original_question: What authentication schemes should be developed for noncommutative group-based cryptography?
target_in_paper: Section 11, Open Problems, General problem 8: "What about the authentication schemes?" Read together with the immediately preceding General problem 7 on digital signatures, this is the nearest official formulation of your draft. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies authentication schemes as the target topic, keeps the scope inside noncommutative/nonabelian group-based cryptography, and asks about constructing new schemes rather than only attacking existing ones. That matches the direction of the paper's open-problem list. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
missing_details: The exact target in the paper is the short open problem in Section 11, General item 8, not a broader request for the "best" or "most secure" authentication method. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

In this paper, authentication is discussed in Section 6 and is closely tied to secure password verification via challenge-response protocols, not to authenticated encryption in general. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Because General item 7 separately asks for more non-commutative digital signatures, the authentication question should be phrased as distinct from the digital-signature question, even though Section 6 notes that authentication often takes the form of a digital signature. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
The paper's concrete authentication model uses a prover/verifier setting and explicitly aims at two-way authentication. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The baseline group-theoretic setup assumes a shared secret consisting of a standard password together with a secret challenge group known to both prover and verifier. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

That challenge group is taken from finitely presented groups with solvable word problem, and the protocol relies on group-randomizer capabilities such as rewriting, normal-form computation, random free-word generation, and subgroup-membership handling. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

Section 6 also includes protocol-level constraints: the verifier should never reuse a submitted challenge word, and legitimacy of the verifier is checked by repeating the process in the opposite direction. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

The security context emphasized for the Section 6 authentication/password-verification method is resistance to ciphertext-only, man-in-the-middle, and replay attacks. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))

No ambient ring/field, degree, homogeneity, nilpotency, or "for all sufficiently large m"-type quantifiers are part of this target problem; the missing stand-alone details are protocol and group-theoretic assumptions instead. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
refined_question: Can one design new non-commutative group-based authentication schemes—distinct from the paper's separately listed problem of constructing more non-commutative digital signatures—and, in particular, secure challenge-response/password-verification protocols that support two-way authentication between prover and verifier, using finitely presented groups with solvable word problem and the group-randomizer/challenge-group framework described in Section 6? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
justification: The nearest official target is Section 11, General problem 8, "What about the authentication schemes?" rather than the neighboring questions about platform groups, public keys, or security measures. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093)) Section 6 gives the intended meaning of "authentication" in this paper: authentication is introduced alongside digital signatures, then developed concretely through secure password verification and challenge-response methods based on combinatorial group theory; the authors specify a prover/verifier model, explicitly mention two-way authentication, and describe a protocol built from secret challenge groups and group-randomizer operations on finitely presented groups with solvable word problem. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093)) Because General problem 7 separately asks for more non-commutative digital signatures, the sharpest paper-faithful rewrite is to ask for new authentication schemes, especially group-based challenge-response/password-verification schemes of the Section 6 type, without broadening to unrelated security-analysis questions. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1103.4093))
